source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2021) Whence the expected free energy?
finding: EFE is not simply the free energy of the future. The natural forward-looking free energy (FEF) actively discourages exploration. The epistemic term only appears in a different objective, FEEF, which the authors propose.
numbers: Theory paper. No sample. FEF vs EFE shown by derivation and small simulations.
quote: it is not simply "the free energy in the future"
limits: Mathematical derivation, not an empirical test. The authors say EFE may still help exploration as a heuristic.
agent_relevance: Do not claim that information-seeking falls out of free energy minimisation. In S7, treat epistemic value as a design choice we add, not a theorem.

source: Millidge et al. (2021) Whence the EFE: limits of Bayes-optimal exploration
finding: Merely quantifying uncertainty with mean-field time steps does not give Bayes-optimal exploration. A true solution needs several linked time steps (active learning).
numbers: Discussion section, no numbers.
limits: Open problem as of 2020.
agent_relevance: One-step info gain is a myopic rule. Consider lookahead only when cheap.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: On FrozenLake with 200 trials over 500 episodes, active inference matched or beat Q-learning and Bayesian model-based RL, mainly in the stochastic variant.
numbers: Deterministic: AIF 99.88 [99.64,100] vs Bayesian RL 99.76 vs Q-learning 97.79 (decaying eps). Stochastic: AIF 98.90 [98.00,99.79] vs Q-learning 66.08, 65.13 and Bayesian RL 64.39.
limits: Tiny toy MDP, authors hand-set preferences. Authors note behaviour depends on the chosen generative model.
agent_relevance: Shows EFE can beat reward-only planners when the task is non-stationary. Small and author-built, so low weight.

source: Sajid et al. (2021) null-preference agent
finding: With no prior preferences the agent only seeks information. It fell in the hole or reached the goal with equal probability, and over time lost purposeful behaviour.
numbers: Null model score 50.03 deterministic, 50.22 stochastic (reward scale 0-100). Goal reached 44.0% of the time.
limits: Shows epistemic value alone has no goal.
agent_relevance: S7 needs a goal term. Choose the test that separates hypotheses AND matters to the answer; pure info gain can chase irrelevant facts.

source: Paul, Sajid, Da Costa, Razi (2024) Reward maximisation through discrete active inference
finding: Standard active inference is Bellman optimal only for planning horizon 1 in POMDPs. Sophisticated inference (recursive) is Bellman optimal on any finite horizon, given exact inference.
numbers: Proofs, no empirical numbers.
quote: standard active inference scheme can produce Bellman optimal actions for planning horizons of 1, but not beyond
limits: Holds for known transitions, exact inference, zero-temperature limit. Real approximate schemes may differ.
agent_relevance: Greedy one-step test selection is the horizon-1 case. Deeper lookahead needs a recursive search over answers.

source: Tschantz, Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2020) Reinforcement learning through active inference
finding: FEEF agent reached the goal in one trial on sparse-reward Mountain Car and beat SAC on well-shaped HalfCheetah after 100 episodes. It covered most of state space where a reward agent stayed in a random-action region.
numbers: Mountain Car: 25 episodes, up to 200 steps each. Ant Maze coverage after 35 episodes, mean of 4 seeds. Compared with SAC and random.
limits: Workshop paper, few seeds, FEEF is not the classic EFE. Directed exploration gave little benefit when reward is well shaped.
agent_relevance: Info-driven choice helps when reward signal is sparse (like a hard puzzle with no partial feedback). Little gain when feedback is dense.

source: Champion, Bowman, Markovic, Grzes (2023) Deconstructing deep active inference
finding: Failed to scale EFE with its information term. On dSprites, only agents that maximised reward solved the task; every agent with the info-gain term failed. The EFE agent picked a single action.
numbers: Five EFE definitions x three action selection rules. Adding even 1% information gain after 200K iterations sharply cut total reward. With softmax sampling all agents failed, one worse than random.
quote: adding even 1% of the information gain already dramatically decreases the amount of reward gathered
limits: One toy environment (dSprites) with a deep CHMM. Could be an implementation issue with the epistemic term.
agent_relevance: Key warning: an epistemic term can swamp the goal term and collapse behaviour. Weight info gain below the answer goal and stop when gain falls near zero (G1).

source: Fountas et al. (2020) Deep active inference agents using Monte-Carlo methods
finding: MCTS-based deep active inference matched reward-based agents in a toy task and in Animal-AI beat DQN and A2C and was comparable to PPO2, with lower variance across runs.
numbers: Animal-AI, 2M learning iterations, default baselines.
limits: Authors say the comparison only shows applicability, not a thorough benchmark. Contrast with Champion et al. on dSprites.
agent_relevance: Tree search over EFE can work, but results are mixed across labs.

source: Sajid, Da Costa, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference, Bayesian optimal design, and expected utility
finding: Dropping preferences from EFE gives Bayesian optimal design (max info gain). Removing ambiguity and relative risk gives expected utility. In a T-maze, EFE gave goal-directed information-seeking, expected utility gave purely exploitive behaviour, info gain alone gave pure curiosity.
numbers: T-maze, reward probability 98% in the context-determined arm.
quote: active inference reduces to optimal Bayesian design, i.e., information gain maximization
limits: Simulation of a single toy task.
agent_relevance: This is the formal link to our S7: 'most separating test' equals the preference-free limit of EFE. Add the answer-goal term to avoid pure curiosity.

source: Millidge (2021) Understanding the origin of information-seeking exploration
finding: Information-seeking arises from divergence objectives (match expected to desired futures), not from evidence/utility objectives. The same view explains probability matching as a non-irrational strategy.
numbers: Theory.
limits: Probability matching explanation is argued, not tested on human data in this paper.
agent_relevance: Supports a divergence-style selection rule: prefer tests that bring the predicted outcome distribution closer to a verified answer state.

source: de Vries, Nuijten et al. (2025) EFE-based planning as variational inference
finding: EFE planning can be derived as variational inference on a generative model augmented with preference and epistemic priors, with a complexity term for bounded compute.
numbers: Theory; simulations only promised in forthcoming work.
limits: No empirical test in the paper.
agent_relevance: The 2025 answer to Millidge's 2020 critique, but still unproven in practice.

source: Schwartenbeck et al. (2019) Computational mechanisms of curiosity and goal-directed exploration
finding: Simulated active inference agents pick informative options. The model needs policy precision that varies with reward size to reproduce the Blanchard et al. (2015) human interaction. No new human data.
numbers: 1,000 simulated experiments of 32 trials in Fig 6; 100 simulations in Fig 10-12.
limits: Only the first 100k of 266k characters of the page were read. No timing or horizon effects predicted. No formal model comparison with participants.
agent_relevance: Human support for EFE is mostly by simulation fit, not by winning a model comparison.

source: Duraisamy (2025) Active inference AI systems for scientific discovery
finding: Position paper arguing active inference suits discovery loops. It proposes an architecture and no benchmark.
numbers: No measured results found in the text read.
limits: Conceptual only.
agent_relevance: Do not count as evidence of benefit.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov, Ellis (2024) Active preference inference using language models and probabilistic reasoning
finding: Choosing the question by expected entropy reduction over an LLM-defined probabilistic model beat vanilla and ReAct LLM questioning in a shopping task. After three questions it exceeded the baselines after four.
numbers: Samples 8 candidate questions per turn. Confidence intervals over 150 settings in the information-gain figure.
limits: Simplified web shopping, simulated user. Expected entropy reduction and expected model change are shown equivalent.
agent_relevance: A direct LLM version of S7: sample candidate tests, score by expected entropy drop in code.

source: Handa, Gal et al. (2024) Bayesian preference elicitation with language models (OPEN)
finding: OPEN picks questions with an EIG objective over LM-extracted features. Open-ended LM questions beat pairwise ones under LM-only evaluation, but the benefit of OPEN's predictor outweighed that.
numbers: Metric is time-integrated delta accuracy. Exact gains not read.
limits: I read the methods and discussion, not all tables. Small user study.
agent_relevance: Information gain over named features works when features can be listed first.

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas (2023) Eliciting human preferences with language models (GATE)
finding: LM-driven elicitation (generative active learning) beat supervised, pool-based active learning and no interaction. Significance was found only in content recommendation and email verification, not the third domain.
numbers: Three domains, metric: area under p(correct) vs interaction time. Users found it less mentally demanding than writing prompts.
limits: Not a formal EIG method. GPT-4 token probabilities unavailable. Result is mixed.
agent_relevance: Even prompted info-seeking helps, but not reliably in every domain.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts
finding: Choosing the next question by simulated information gain raised success rate by 38.1% on average over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs. Llama3-70B gained 46.6%.
numbers: Beat CoT-SC by 33.8%, Reflexion by 29.9%, original ToT by 28.3%, adapted ToT by 12.4%. DX diagnosis 97.0% with GPT-4. Troubleshooting 43.7% to 67.3% with GPT-4.
limits: Answers simulated by GPT-4. Simplified benchmarks. Questions that do not fully eliminate options break the model. Depth limited to three steps.
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM evidence that code-scored information gain beats free prompting. Matches S7. Check that the answerer is not the same model as the questioner.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT ablation of reward design and propagation
finding: Information-gain reward beat the ToT self-evaluation reward at comparable efficiency. One-step planning already captures most of the benefit; they limit simulation to three steps.
numbers: Reward ablation tables on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Numbers vary by dataset.
limits: Cost-limited experiments.
agent_relevance: Cheap one-step scoring is sufficient; deep trees add cost.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu, van der Schaar (2025) Active task disambiguation with LLMs
finding: EIG-based clarifying questions beat implicit question reasoning for code tasks. At t=10 questions (HumanEval, GPT-3.5): EIG-uniform 6.2 vs EIG-logprobs 4.1 vs implicit-ToT 5.1 vs implicit 4.9. The gap shrinks for more capable models.
numbers: HumanEval 48 tasks, APPS 47 tasks, 3 runs and 3 eval seeds. GPT-4o-mini at t=10: 6.8 vs 6.0, 6.6, 5.5.
limits: Absolute accuracy gains small (a few points). Logprob-weighted EIG sometimes worse than uniform. Open questions need more user effort.
agent_relevance: Gains are modest and shrink with model strength, so test on our model before trusting S7 value.

source: Grand et al. (2026) Shoot first, ask questions later? Collaborative Battleship (ICLR 2026)
finding: Human data: asking questions correlated with performance. Bayesian EIG-based question choice lifted expected information gain up to 0.227 bits (94.2% of the noise ceiling) and made weak models beat humans.
numbers: 42 human players, 126 games. Llama-4-Scout F1 0.367 to 0.764; GPT-4o 0.450 to 0.782; win rate vs humans 8% to 82%. 54 games per captain. Redundant questions (EIG=0): 18.5% to 0.2% (Scout), 14.6% to 1.2% (GPT-4o).
limits: Single game family plus a Guess Who? replication (+28.3 to +42.4 pp). Spotter fixed to GPT-5.
agent_relevance: Best LLM test of our exact rule: pick the question with max EIG in code.

source: Grand et al. (2026) high EIG alone not sufficient
finding: Question choice by EIG alone barely improved game play. Only marginalising question implications into the move choice brought gains.
numbers: QBayes alone: +0.021 to +0.026 F1 for Scout and GPT-4o despite large EIG gains. Weak models front-load all 15 questions; humans and GPT-5 ask 8.0-8.2 vs 14.1-14.9.
limits: Authors suggest weak models cannot turn info into moves.
agent_relevance: Selecting the best test is not enough. The update step (S8) must be done in code, and questions must be budgeted over time.

source: Grand et al. (2026) LM question and answer quality vs humans
finding: Many LMs ask poor questions and answer worse than humans. Human spotter accuracy 92.5%. Code generation closes much of the answer gap. Context-dependent questions are hard for LMs.
numbers: Human spotter accuracy 92.5%; complex questions 87.4% vs 91.9% for the best code-based setting.
limits: Different LMs vary widely.
agent_relevance: Let the program compute answers from state, as in G2 and G5, instead of asking the model to judge.

source: Sajid et al. (2021) Pepper: reward-free preference learning
finding: Learned preferences in a constant FrozenLake become precise and exploit. In volatile settings, preference uncertainty keeps exploration alive.
numbers: FrozenLake and 3D mini-world, with and without volatility.
limits: Qualitative simulations; only abstract and setup read.
agent_relevance: Exploration is best driven by uncertainty about the goal, not on a timer (matches G1).

source: Paul et al. (2024) practical caveat on exact vs approximate inference
finding: Authors say sophisticated inference will vastly outperform standard active inference in most reward tasks, but only if inference is accurate.
numbers: No numbers; stated as expectation.
limits: Prediction, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Treat claimed advantages of deeper EFE search as unverified.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT limitation on overlapping answers
finding: The info-gain calculation assumes yes and no answers split the hypothesis set cleanly. In practice an answer like 'no fever' does not remove COVID entirely.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Authors give no corrected figures.
agent_relevance: Use soft likelihoods per hypothesis, not hard partitions, when computing separation.

source: Piriyakulkij et al. (2024) equivalence of entropy and model change
finding: Expected entropy minimisation and expected model change maximisation are equivalent in their setup, since the expected cross-entropy term is the same for all questions.
numbers: Derivation in Appendix A.1.
limits: Holds under their probabilistic model.
agent_relevance: One implementation of S7 is enough; do not run two scoring rules.

source: Evidence gap: human experimental tests of EFE
finding: I did not find a large human replication or meta-analysis that pits EFE against reward or information-gain models. The web search budget was exhausted, so this is a gap in my search, not proof of absence.
numbers: None found.
limits: Friston et al. 2015 was not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat human evidence for EFE as weak until a model comparison with participants is found.
